summary:
We developed Ghosts of Exploration, a free, story-driven website about 49 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and across the solar system. Visitors start with Echo’s journey, a 5-minute narrated story told by Echo, the last radio message a spacecraft ever sends home. Then each machine tells its own story in a first-person “ghost log” built from NASA records, and appears on a map at its true coordinates. Every machine also has a cartoon short, a comic and a podcast episode. Kids can walk 14 real landing sites in 3D and play games with real gravity and signal delay.

This answers the challenge by turning dense mission records into narrative. Step-by-step animations show how the hardware worked, and every dossier links the engineering to the science it made possible. Every fact is checked against NASA and NSSDCA sources.

It matters because kids usually hear only about active missions. These retired machines made today’s discoveries possible, and their stories teach persistence and why missions end. The site is free, works offline, comes in English, Spanish and Hindi, and includes a teacher pack, so any classroom can use it.
details:
What it does and how it works
Ghosts of Exploration is a free website that gives a voice to 49 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and across the solar system. Visitors start with Echo’s journey, a 5-minute narrated story told by Echo, the last radio message a spacecraft ever sends home, as it travels at the speed of light from the Moon to interstellar space. Then every machine has its own dossier: a first-person “ghost log”, an epitaph, planned vs. actual results, discoveries, NASA photos, and its own cartoon short, comic and podcast episode. Kids find the machines on a map at their true coordinates, watch step-by-step animations of how they landed, walk 14 real landing sites in 3D, and play games with real gravity and signal delay. One data file of checked facts powers everything, so a fact corrected once is right everywhere.

Benefits
Dense mission records become stories children remember. Every fact links to NASA and NSSDCA sources, so teachers can trust it. Teachers also get NGSS-linked lesson plans, worksheets and a class quiz at no cost. The site works offline, on phones, and needs no sign-up.

Intended impact
Kids usually hear only about active missions. We want them to learn that today’s discoveries stand on the shoulders of retired machines like Viking, Spirit and Opportunity, and why missions end, sometimes on purpose: Cassini and Galileo were steered into their planets to protect moons that might hold life. We want them to feel a personal connection to these explorers, and to see persistence and curiosity in their stories.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript on GitHub Pages, with no servers. We also used:

  • Three.js, Google’s model-viewer and a Unity WebGL player for 3D;
  • Blender and ffmpeg to generate all 49 cartoon shorts from our data;
  • Python and Node.js for build scripts, and text-to-speech for narration;
  • an optional Cloudflare Worker with Google’s Gemini for the Ask page.

Creativity
One checked archive becomes many formats: a guided story, comics, a podcast, cartoons, games and 3D walks. Echo, our original character, turns the speed of light into the storyteller, and each machine speaks in its own voice. The cartoon shorts are generated from the same facts, so the art always matches the science.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: sourced facts, myths corrected, estimates labelled.
  • Age: two reading levels for ages 8–14.
  • Accessibility: read-aloud, captions, dyslexia-friendly text, keyboard support and reduced motion.
  • Reach: English, Spanish and Hindi, offline use for low-bandwidth classrooms, and no ads or tracking.
  • Cost: free to use and free to host.
